summary: Responds to RFC 603 on network connectivity. The author argues that what matters in judging a node with four links is how well the network stays connected after the node fails, not how many circuits are affected, and addresses the points raised there.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 613 responds to a debate about ARPANET connections. It argues that reliability depends on whether the remaining network stays connected after a node fails, not simply on the number of circuits affected.

today: The unit records RFC 613's status as Unknown and says it updates RFC 603. It is a discussion of network connectivity and topology.

sections.title: The Question of Network Connectivity
sections.content:
Alex McKenzie describes network topology as a political and economic question with technical aspects. He limits the memo to responding to points raised in RFC 603.

One question in that discussion is whether it is good or bad for a node such as AMES to have four connections.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo answers selected points from RFC 603 rather than covering every argument about network design. One issue is how many connections a node should have.

sections.title: Judge the Network After a Failure
sections.content:
McKenzie says a four-connected node should be judged by how well the network remains connected if that node fails, not by how many circuits the failure affects. He argues that four-connected nodes are not the main weakness; one-connected and two-connected nodes are.

He agrees that two adjacent three-connected nodes are preferable to a four-connected node next to a two-connected node. He adds that practical limits on installing interfaces and common-carrier services can lead the network to expand in less-than-optimal ways.
sections.plainLanguage: A node with few connections may leave the network divided if it fails. The author says to consider the connections that remain, rather than count only the circuits attached to the failed node.

sections.title: Loops, Circuits and Long Chains
sections.content:
The author says loops are not inherently good; they help because they increase connectivity and reduce the effects of multiple failures. Additional circuits cost money for IMP interfaces and recurring circuit service.

BBN had recommended increasing connectivity and, in late December 1973, proposed specific locations for additional circuits. The proposals aimed to break up long chains of IMPs that had formed as the network grew. The author says ARPA and NAC were presumably evaluating those suggestions.
sections.plainLanguage: A loop is useful when it adds alternate connections, but adding circuits costs money. BBN proposed places for new circuits to break up long chains of IMPs.

references.text: RFC 603, the document to which RFC 613 responds.
